newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German workers closer to strikes in Bavaria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German workers closer to strikes in Bavaria.

text.p: Regional leaders of the IG Metall union in Bavaria, home to some of Germany's most powerful companies, on Thursday gave the clearest signal yet of its readiness to strike over planned cuts to sick pay benefits.

With membership at around half of the 700,000 workers in the region's metal and electronics sectors, strike action could hit hard industrial giants such as Siemens, Bayerische Motorenwerke (BMW) and Volkswagen's Audi.

IG Metall said in a statement that it would hold a formal vote next month on whether to cancel existing wage contracts from early next year, a move that would then legally give it the option of strike action.

The union's central leadership separately announced in Wuppertal, near Cologne, that they were planning a country-wide day of protest against the proposed cuts and also refused to rule out strike action.

The moves follow a rash of announcements by large companies over the last two days, led by vehicle-maker Daimler-Benz AG, that they planned to cut sick pay entitlements in accordance with new laws passed earlier this month.
Siemens and engineering group Mannesmann AG were also among the companies that said they were planning to adopt the new measures on sick pay.
IG Metall regional director Werner Neugebauer said that after having discussed the proposed cuts with the companies involved, the employers had changed their position "not one millimetre".

A spokesman for IG Metall in Bavaria said that agreements on sick pay entitlements -- payable at 100 percent of salary -- stood as "autonomus clauses" within existing wage agreements and could not therefore be over-ruled by the new laws.
These are designed to allow German firms, which argue that the sick payments are one of many over-generous benefits stifling competitiveness, to cut them to 80 percent of salary.
IG Metall will formally vote on the cancelling of the contracts on October 24 and if -- as expected -- the vote is carried, strike action could be planned from early February.
Siemens, around 170,000 of whose employees country-wide would be affected by the changes, said it had no immediate comment on the IG Metall statement.

A spokesman for BMW, which was not among those companies that announced their plans, said it was still seeking to reach agreement with worker groups on ways to put the new law into effect in a way more acceptable to employees.

Signs of unrest at the cuts were seen elswhere across the country, with some 25,000 workers at factories owned by Daimler's Mercedes unit laying down tools in protest, while banking unions said that strikes were legally open to as an option.
